noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to draw dot-and-cross diagrams to show electrons in covalent substances, including: i molecules with single, double and triple bonds ii species with dative covalent (coordinate) bonds, including Al 2 Cl 6 and the ammonium ion

primer.text: Shared pairs come in singles, doubles, triples - and donations. Dot-and-cross diagrams track every electron's origin; oxygen doubles up, nitrogen triples, and a lone pair can fund an entire bond to an electron-deficient partner, as ammonia does to H+ and two AlCl3 molecules do to each other. This note drills the diagrams, bond orders and dative cases.

lessons.title: Diagrams of the shared deal
lessons.opening: Covalent compounds fill outer shells by pooling rather than transferring: each atom contributes electrons to shared pairs, and every partner counts the shared electrons toward a noble-gas arrangement. Dot-and-cross diagrams record the deal - dots for one atom's electrons, crosses for the other's, drawn only in the outer shells.
keyPoints: Atoms in covalent compounds share their outer valence electrons to reach noble gas configurations.
Each shared pair is counted by both atoms toward a full outer shell.
Dot-and-cross diagrams show only outer-shell electrons, with symbols distinguishing each atom's contribution.
Unlike ionic diagrams, covalent drawings need no brackets or corner charges.
The periodic table tells you how many outer electrons each non-metal brings to the deal.

low.restatement: Non-metal atoms lend electrons into joint pairs; both partners count each pair as their own until every shell reads full.
low.analogy: Two students each holding half a library card: neither owns it alone, but together they borrow as one full member.
low.examPointer: Use the periodic table for outer-electron counts - group number gives the contribution each atom brings.

medium.restatement: The shared-pair economy lets each atom claim octet completion without ownership change: dot-and-cross diagrams track the origin of every electron so the examiner can audit the count around each nucleus.
medium.analogy: A joint bank account with colour-coded deposits: the money is shared, but the ledger remembers who paid what in.
medium.examPointer: Audit each atom in your diagram: count dots plus crosses around every nucleus and confirm the octet before moving on.

check.stem: What do covalent compounds do with their outer valence electrons?

options.text: Share them in pairs to achieve noble gas configurations
options.explanation: Pooling completes the outer shells of both partners.

options.text: Transfer them completely to one atom
options.explanation: Full transfer defines ionic bonding.

options.text: Delete them to empty the shell
options.explanation: Electrons are conserved, never deleted.

options.text: Hide them in the nucleus
options.explanation: Electrons stay outside the nucleus.

check.stem: In a covalent dot-and-cross diagram, what distinguishes the two atoms' electrons?

options.text: Dots for one atom's electrons and crosses for the other's
options.explanation: The two symbols track electron origin.

options.text: Red versus blue shading only
options.explanation: The convention uses dots and crosses.

options.text: Numbers written beside each electron
options.explanation: Symbols, not numbers, carry the distinction.

options.text: Nothing - all electrons look identical
options.explanation: Origin tracking is the diagram's point.

check.stem: How does a covalent dot-and-cross diagram differ from an ionic one?

options.text: No brackets or ionic charges appear - the atoms stay neutral sharing partners
options.explanation: Covalent species are molecules, not bracketed charged ions.

options.text: Ionic diagrams show no electrons at all
options.explanation: Both diagram types show outer electrons.

options.text: Covalent diagrams include inner shells
options.explanation: Both types draw outer shells only.

options.text: Only ionic diagrams use crosses
options.explanation: Both use the dot-cross convention.

check.stem: Why does sharing let each atom reach a noble gas configuration?

options.text: Each atom counts the shared pairs as part of its own outer shell
options.explanation: Joint ownership completes the octet without transfer.

options.text: Sharing removes excess electrons entirely
options.explanation: Nothing is removed; pairs are pooled.

options.text: The atoms physically merge into one atom
options.explanation: Atoms stay distinct nuclei.

options.text: The noble gas atom donates the electrons
options.explanation: No third party exists in a two-atom bond.

check.stem: A chlorine atom has seven outer electrons. How many shared pairs must it form with hydrogen atoms to complete its octet in HCl?

options.text: One shared pair - one electron from each atom completes chlorine's octet
options.explanation: Seven plus one shared partner electron reaches eight.

options.text: Two shared pairs
options.explanation: That would overfill to nine.

options.text: Three shared pairs
options.explanation: That would reach eleven.

options.text: None - chlorine already has a full shell
options.explanation: Seven is one short of the octet.

check.stem: State what atoms in covalent compounds do with their outer valence electrons.
check.modelAnswer: They share their outer valence electrons in pairs to achieve a noble gas configuration.

check.stem: State the two drawing rules of covalent dot-and-cross diagrams.
check.modelAnswer: Show only outer-shell electrons, and use dots versus crosses to mark which atom each electron came from.

check.stem: Explain why covalent diagrams need no square brackets or ionic charges.
check.modelAnswer: Covalent bonding produces neutral molecules in which electrons are shared, not transferred, so no ion forms - and brackets exist in diagrams precisely to carry ionic charge.

check.stem: Use the periodic table to give the outer-electron contribution of H, Cl and O, then predict the formula each completes an octet in with single bonds.
check.modelAnswer: H brings one, Cl seven, O six: one H-Cl pair completes both (HCl), and oxygen needs two single partners (H2O) to reach its octet.

lessons.title: Doubling and tripling up
lessons.opening: Some atoms need more than one shared pair to complete their shells. Oxygen gas pairs its atoms with a double bond, carbon dioxide wires each oxygen to carbon doubly, and ethene joins its two carbons doubly. Nitrogen goes one better still: its triple bond pools three pairs between the two atoms.
keyPoints: A double covalent bond shares two pairs of electrons between two atoms.
O2 carries one double bond; CO2 carries two, one to each oxygen; ethene's carbons join by C=C.
A triple covalent bond shares three pairs, as in N2.
Multiple bonds arise when single pairs would leave an atom short of its octet.
Each double bond counts as two shared pairs - four electrons; a triple bond is six.

low.restatement: When one shared pair is not enough, atoms pool two or even three pairs between them - drawing two or three connecting lines.
low.analogy: Handshakes becoming arm-wrestles: two arms locked (double bond) or three ropes tied (triple bond) bind the partners far more tightly.
low.examPointer: Count electrons per bond type aloud: single 2, double 4, triple 6 - the counting is the mark.

medium.restatement: Bond order tracks electron debt: oxygen's six valence electrons need two shared pairs to octet, nitrogen's five need three; CO2 and ethene merely relocate the same double-bond logic into larger frameworks.
medium.analogy: Instalment plans: the bigger the missing share of the octet, the more instalments - pairs - the bond must transfer into the joint account.
medium.examPointer: In diagrams, every bond line equals one pair: audit the count around each atom line by line.

check.stem: How many shared pairs make up a double covalent bond?

options.text: Two pairs - four shared electrons
options.explanation: Two lines between the atoms represent them.

options.text: One pair - two electrons
options.explanation: That is a single bond.

options.text: Three pairs - six electrons
options.explanation: That is a triple bond.

options.text: Four pairs - eight electrons
options.explanation: No common bond order reaches four pairs here.

check.stem: What holds the two oxygen atoms together in O2?

options.text: A double covalent bond sharing two pairs
options.explanation: Each oxygen contributes two electrons to the joint pool.

options.text: A single covalent bond
options.explanation: One pair would leave both oxygens short of an octet.

options.text: A triple covalent bond
options.explanation: Triples belong to nitrogen's diatomic molecule.

options.text: An ionic bond between oxide ions
options.explanation: O2 is a neutral molecule.

check.stem: How do the bonds in CO2 connect carbon to each oxygen?

options.text: Each oxygen is double-bonded to the carbon
options.explanation: Two C=O bonds complete every octet in the molecule.

options.text: Each oxygen is single-bonded to the carbon
options.explanation: Singles would strand both partners short.

options.text: One oxygen doubles, the other singles
options.explanation: The molecule is symmetric with two double bonds.

options.text: The oxygens bond to each other, not the carbon
options.explanation: The structure is O=C=O.

check.stem: How many shared pairs does the bond in N2 contain?

options.text: Three pairs - a triple bond
options.explanation: Each nitrogen supplies three electrons, pooling six in total.

options.text: One pair
options.explanation: One pair leaves each nitrogen five electrons short.

options.text: Two pairs
options.explanation: Two pairs leave each nitrogen two electrons short.

options.text: Four pairs
options.explanation: No fourth pair is needed once the octet completes.

check.stem: Ethene's two carbon atoms are joined by a bond containing how many electrons?

options.text: Four electrons - a double bond
options.explanation: The C=C linkage shares two pairs.

options.text: Two electrons - a single bond
options.explanation: Ethene's carbons share more than one pair.

options.text: Six electrons - a triple bond
options.explanation: Triple bonds belong to N2 in this syllabus set.

options.text: Eight electrons
options.explanation: That exceeds any two-atom shared pool here.

check.stem: Define a double covalent bond.
check.modelAnswer: A double covalent bond shares two pairs of electrons - four electrons in total - between two atoms.

check.stem: Name the molecules from the note that carry double bonds and the one that carries a triple bond.
check.modelAnswer: O2, CO2 and ethene carry double bonds; nitrogen, N2, carries a triple bond.

check.stem: Explain why nitrogen needs a triple bond rather than a single bond.
check.modelAnswer: Each nitrogen atom carries five valence electrons, three short of an octet; pooling three pairs - one more than a single or double bond supplies - lets both atoms complete their outer shells.

check.stem: Count the total shared electrons in one CO2 molecule across all its bonds.
check.modelAnswer: Two double bonds each carry four shared electrons, giving eight shared electrons in total across the molecule.

lessons.title: The dative bond: one-sided donations
lessons.opening: Some bonds are funded by one partner alone. When an atom with a lone pair meets an electron-deficient atom with an unfilled orbital, the whole shared pair can come from the donor - a dative covalent, or coordinate, bond. The ammonium ion is the classic: ammonia's lone pair lands on a bare proton. Aluminium chloride plays the same game twice over, dimerising into Al2Cl6 when two AlCl3 molecules swap lone-pair donations.
keyPoints: A dative covalent bond forms when a lone pair is donated to an electron-deficient atom.
An electron-deficient atom has an unfilled outer orbital.
In a dative bond both shared electrons come from the same donor atom.
Ammonia donates its lone pair to H+ to form the ammonium ion, NH4+.
Two AlCl3 molecules dimerise to Al2Cl6 at lower temperatures via two chlorine-to-aluminium coordinate bonds.

low.restatement: Normally each partner funds half a bond; in a dative bond one atom funds the whole pair and hands it to a partner with a spare slot.
low.analogy: Buying a cinema seat for a friend who arrived cashless: the seat is shared, but one wallet paid for it.
low.examPointer: Arrow notation points from donor to acceptor - draw the arrow head on the electron-deficient atom.

medium.restatement: Dative bonding repairs octet deficits pair-by-pair: the donor's lone pair fills the acceptor's empty orbital, converting AlCl3's electron poverty at low temperature into a four-coordinate dimer held by two coordinate links.
medium.analogy: A key-cutting kiosk (donor) slotting a spare key (lone pair) into a friend's empty lock (unfilled orbital) - the door then opens for both.
medium.examPointer: State the temperature condition for AlCl3: monomer at high temperature, dimer Al2Cl6 at lower temperature.

check.stem: What is required for a dative covalent bond to form?

options.text: A lone pair on one atom and an unfilled orbital on the other
options.explanation: The donor fills the acceptor's empty slot.

options.text: Two atoms each holding spare electrons
options.explanation: Only one atom donates.

options.text: A metal and a non-metal pair
options.explanation: Dative bonds appear in covalent systems like NH4+.

options.text: A full octet on both atoms beforehand
options.explanation: The acceptor is precisely octet-short.

check.stem: In the ammonium ion, which species donates the electron pair?

options.text: The nitrogen atom of ammonia, donating its lone pair to H+
options.explanation: N's lone pair becomes the fourth N-H bonding pair.

options.text: The hydrogen ion, donating its electron to nitrogen
options.explanation: H+ carries no electrons to donate.

options.text: Both share one electron each
options.explanation: The dative pair comes from one side only.

options.text: A chloride ion floating nearby
options.explanation: No chloride participates in NH4+ formation.

check.stem: Why is the hydrogen ion described as electron-deficient?

options.text: Its outer shell has space for two electrons it does not yet hold
options.explanation: A bare proton accepts a pair into its empty shell.

options.text: It carries a negative charge
options.explanation: H+ is positively charged.

options.text: It has too many electrons
options.explanation: Deficiency means too few, not too many.

options.text: It refuses to bond with anything
options.explanation: Bonding with the lone pair is exactly its appetite.

check.stem: What happens to aluminium chloride molecules at lower temperatures?

options.text: Two AlCl3 monomers join into an Al2Cl6 dimer via two coordinate bonds
options.explanation: Chlorine lone pairs donate into both electron-deficient aluminium centres.

options.text: They break apart into ions
options.explanation: The bonding stays covalent and dative.

options.text: They remain monomers at all temperatures
options.explanation: Temperature decides monomer versus dimer.

options.text: They gain extra chlorine atoms permanently
options.explanation: The formula stays Al2Cl6 - just two original units joined.

check.stem: Why is the monomer AlCl3 described as electron-deficient?

options.text: The aluminium atom's outer shell lacks two electrons of a full octet
options.explanation: Three bonds supply six electrons; two more would complete it.

options.text: Aluminium has lost all its electrons
options.explanation: It shares three pairs with chlorine.

options.text: The chlorines refuse to share
options.explanation: Three Cl atoms do share pairs with Al.

options.text: The molecule carries a negative charge
options.explanation: AlCl3 is neutral.

check.stem: Define dative covalent bonding.
check.modelAnswer: Dative covalent (coordinate) bonding forms when one atom donates a lone pair to an electron-deficient atom, with both shared electrons coming from the same atom.

check.stem: State the formulae of the ammonium ion and the aluminium chloride dimer.
check.modelAnswer: The ammonium ion is NH4+, formed from NH3 and H+; the aluminium chloride dimer is Al2Cl6.

check.stem: Explain why both electrons of a dative bond are said to come from the same atom.
check.modelAnswer: In a normal covalent bond each partner contributes one electron to the pair; in a dative bond the acceptor arrives with no electrons of its own to contribute, so the donor's pre-existing lone pair supplies the entire shared pair.

check.stem: Track the bond count around nitrogen when NH3 becomes NH4+: state how many bonds and from where each electron pair comes.
check.modelAnswer: Nitrogen ends with four N-H bonds: three ordinary covalent pairs funded half by N and half by H, plus one dative pair funded wholly by nitrogen's lone pair, landing on the electron-deficient proton.

glossary.definition: A bond sharing two pairs of electrons - four electrons - between two atoms, drawn as two lines.
A bond sharing three pairs of electrons - six in total - as in N2.
A coordinate bond whose shared pair comes entirely from one donor atom's lone pair.
Describing an atom with an unfilled outer orbital, ready to accept a donated pair.
